knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Cartesian Function With Respect to Plane Polar Coordinates

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2xy+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\sin\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\cos\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\sin\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\cos\theta +2r\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta} & =-2r\sin\theta \,r\sin\theta +(2r\cos\theta +2r\sin\theta )r\cos\theta  \\ & =2{r}^{2}(\cos^{2}\theta -\sin^{2}\theta )+{r}^{2}\sin(2\theta) \\ & =2{r}^{2}\cos(2\theta)+{r}^{2}\sin(2\theta)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x, y) = \ln (x + y)$, find $\frac{∂g}{∂r}$, where $(x, y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r, \theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cos\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta })\cos\theta +(\frac{1}{r\cos\theta +r\sin\theta })\sin\theta  \\ & =\frac{(\cos\theta +\sin\theta )}{r(\cos\theta +\sin\theta )} \\ & =\frac{1}{r}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cos\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\cos\theta \sin\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\cos\theta \sin\theta )\cos\theta +({r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta )\sin\theta  \\ & =2{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta \sin\theta +{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta \sin\theta  \\ & =3{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta \sin\theta \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\ln({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cos\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\cos\theta }{{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\sin\theta }{{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =(\frac{2r\cos\theta }{{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta })\cos\theta +(\frac{2r\sin\theta }{{r}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta })\sin\theta  \\ & =\frac{2r(\cos^{2}\theta +\sin^{2}\theta )}{{r}^{2}(\cos^{2}\theta +\sin^{2}\theta )} \\ & =\frac{2}{r}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cos\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\cos\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\cos\theta )\cos\theta +0\,(\sin\theta ) \\ & =2r\cos^{2}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)={y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\cos\theta $ and $y=r\sin\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\sin\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\cos\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta} & =0\,(-r\sin\theta )+(2r\sin\theta )\,r\cos\theta  \\ & ={r}^{2}\sin(2\theta)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2},$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =r\cos\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\sin\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta} & =-(r\cos\theta )\,r\sin\theta +(r\sin\theta )\,r\cos\theta  \\ & =-{r}^{2}\sin\theta \cos\theta +{r}^{2}\sin\theta \cos\theta  \\ & =0\end{aligned}
$$
